person.name: Heinz_Nixdorf
person.summary: Heinz Nixdorf built a German computer company around compact systems for business data processing. He founded Nixdorf Computer AG and expanded it from a small laboratory into an international electronics company.

conclusion: Heinz Nixdorf's System 820 helped establish decentralized electronic data processing for midsize businesses. Nixdorf Computer's banking, retail, and business systems continued through later corporate successors, including Siemens Nixdorf and Wincor Nixdorf.

events.title: Birth in Paderborn
events.description: Heinz Nixdorf is born in Paderborn as the eldest of five children. His father, Walter Nixdorf, works for the railroad. Periods of his unemployment leave the family with little money.

events.title: Wins School Scholarship
events.description: A scholarship allows Heinz Nixdorf to attend teacher-training schools in Vallendar, Boppard, and Alfeld from 1939 to 1942. He does not want to become a teacher. In 1941, the Ministry of Education permits him to attend Reismann Gymnasium in Paderborn.

events.date_note: His Nazi Party membership was dated retroactively to April 20, 1943
events.title: Enters Wartime Service
events.description: In 1943, Heinz Nixdorf enters the [[Reich Labor Service|Reich Labor Service]]. He is drafted to a [[Luftwaffe|Luftwaffe]] school on the Ith in the Weser Uplands. He applies for membership in the [[Nazi Party|Nazi Party]] on June 1. At the school, he earns all three glider pilot licenses.

Reich Labor Service.explanation: The Reich Labor Service was a compulsory labor and training organization of Nazi Germany. Nixdorf entered it before his military training.

Luftwaffe.explanation: The Luftwaffe was Nazi Germany's air force. Nixdorf attended one of its schools, where he completed glider training.

Nazi Party.explanation: The Nazi Party was the political organization that ruled Germany under Adolf Hitler from 1933 to 1945. Nixdorf applied for membership during his training in 1943.

events.title: Returns to Paderborn
events.description: After the Luftwaffe armored division Hermann Göring is defeated in Bohemia, Heinz Nixdorf escapes capture. He returns to Paderborn in May 1945. His father had died on the Eastern Front in 1944. Nixdorf works in agriculture to help support his mother and siblings.

Panzer-Division Hermann Göring.explanation: The Panzer-Division Hermann Göring was a German armored formation of the Luftwaffe that fought on several fronts during World War II.

events.background:
The Nixdorfs had already moved between regions before the war disrupted Heinz’s schooling. Walter Nixdorf’s work took the family from Paderborn to Torgau in Saxony soon after Heinz’s birth. They returned to Paderborn in 1931. Heinz first attended a Catholic elementary school, where he showed an aptitude for mathematics and science. A scholarship earned through strong schoolwork placed him in teacher-training institutions from 1939 through 1942. He studied in Vallendar near Koblenz, then Boppard on the Rhine, and finally Alfeld on the Leine. The course led toward teaching, a career he did not want.

Heinz pressed his case against his mother’s and teachers’ wishes. He submitted a petition to the Ministry of Education in Berlin. The ministry granted permission in 1941 for him to transfer to Reismann Gymnasium in Paderborn. His education did not proceed directly to a final examination. He reached the Reich Labor Service in 1943 and then the Luftwaffe school on the Ith in the Weser Uplands. He applied for Nazi Party membership on June 1, 1943. The party admitted him retroactively from April 20 under membership number 9,595,797.

The wartime break delayed his university entrance qualification until 1947. Reismann Gymnasium was the school at which he completed it. A scholarship then enabled him to leave Paderborn for Goethe University Frankfurt, where he studied applied physics and also attended business-administration seminars. The route into physics had begun with a fight to leave teacher training. It later brought him into Remington Rand’s development department as a working student in 1951.

events.title: Begins Physics Studies
events.description: In 1947, Heinz Nixdorf completes the [[Abitur|German university-entrance examination]] at Reismann Gymnasium in Paderborn. With a scholarship, he begins studying applied physics at Goethe University Frankfurt. He also attends seminars in business administration.

Abitur.explanation: The Abitur is Germany's secondary-school leaving examination and qualification for university study.

events.title: Joins Remington Rand
events.description: In 1951, Heinz Nixdorf becomes a working student in the development department of Remington Rand’s German subsidiary. He helps develop simple multiplying and accounting machines. He becomes an assistant to physicist Walter Sprick, the department’s director.

events.title: Founds Impulse Laboratory
events.description: In 1952, Heinz Nixdorf leaves his physics studies in his ninth semester. RWE, an electricity company in Essen, provides 30,000 marks for a tube-based calculating machine. Nixdorf founds the Heinz Nixdorf Laboratory for Impulse Technology in Essen. Walter Sprick guarantees the funding and transfers his inventions and patent to Nixdorf.

events.background:
Business calculation in West Germany still relied heavily on punched-card equipment and electromechanical office machines. Tabulating machines could sort and print data from punched cards. Their gear- and relay-driven mechanisms handled multiplication and division slowly. Large manufacturers such as IBM dominated the computer market with mainframes. The smaller-business market for accounting and calculation equipment remained open to compact machines.

Walter Sprick had already built a working example of the technical approach behind the laboratory. While financing his doctoral work at the University of Kiel, he developed an electronic calculator for the Schleswig-Holstein State Fire Insurance Fund. It was completed in 1951. The system paired a tube-based auxiliary machine, which performed decimal multiplication and division quickly, with a tabulating machine. The tabulating machine supplied the existing punched-card workflow. Sprick’s construction was Germany’s first tube computer put to practical use.

The work also drew on a second line of Sprick’s research. By 1952, he had developed a method for optically scanning written characters. A German patent for the character-reading process was dated June 29, 1952. The technique traced the contours of scanned characters as electrical signals. IBM later issued its IBM 1287 multifunction reader in 1966 using work taken up by Evon C. Greanias.

The first laboratory staff member was Alfred Wierzoich, a trained radio and television technician, who began work on September 1, 1952. A friend supplied a further 10,000 Deutsche Marks. The laboratory’s early work grew out of a need for faster accounting calculation while preserving punched-card data handling. Its first delivered system used tube electronics to process information stored on punched cards for RWE’s accounting operation.

events.title: Delivers the ES Computer
events.description: In early 1954, the Heinz Nixdorf Laboratory for Impulse Technology delivers the ES to RWE’s accounting department in Essen. Heinz Nixdorf directs its development with Alfred Wierzoich. Walter Sprick provides technical assistance based on his earlier work.

event_class.title: ES electronic calculator
event_class.description: Vacuum tubes and punched cards performed bookkeeping calculations through electronically controlled arithmetic circuits for RWE's accounting department.
event_class.impact: It gave the laboratory a working machine for a major industrial customer.

events.title: Moves to Paderborn
events.description: In 1959, Heinz Nixdorf moves his company headquarters from Essen to his hometown of Paderborn. Paderborn offers more room for expansion. It also offers a larger pool of available workers.

events.title: Unveils Wanderer Logatronic at Hanover Fair
events.description: In 1965, Heinz Nixdorf presents the Wanderer Logatronic at the Hanover Fair in Hanover. Development engineer Otto Müller designs the modular desk computer. It uses [[semiconductors|solid-state electronic components]]. The Logatronic gives Nixdorf’s company its own small-computer product.

semiconductors.explanation: Semiconductors are electronic materials whose conductivity can be controlled, allowing them to function as components such as transistors. Their use made the Logatronic a smaller solid-state computer than earlier tube-based machines.

events.title: Launches System 820
events.description: In 1967, Nixdorf’s company develops the Wanderer Logatronic into the Nixdorf System 820 in Paderborn. Otto Müller leads the development. Heinz Nixdorf builds a sales network to offer the system directly to midsize businesses.

event_class.title: Nixdorf System 820
event_class.description: A freely programmable small computer paired magnetic-core memory, an integrated keyboard, and typewriter output in a modular system.
event_class.impact: The system established Nixdorf as a supplier of decentralized electronic data processing.

events.background:
By the mid-1960s, the Laboratory for Impulse Technology was still exposed to the fortunes of the office-machine companies that sold its components. Orders from the Wanderer Works had fallen. The French manufacturer Bull was in financial trouble and sharply reduced its calls for equipment. The resulting excess capacity placed the Paderborn business under severe pressure. Kienzle-Apparate GmbH of Villingen offered to absorb the laboratory and make Nixdorf head of its development department. He sought to preserve the company’s independence while it needed a product with its own customers.

Otto Müller had already pursued the idea of a compact computer before arriving in Paderborn. At Telefunken, he and his wife had offered the nearly completed TR 10, a machine Telefunken judged too small for its interests. He then worked at IBM’s Research Center in the United States. Nixdorf recruited the Müllers back to Germany in 1964. Müller’s earlier experience fit the opening that the large computer makers left in business data processing. IBM and other global firms focused on mainframes. Many medium-sized companies still needed equipment for accounting and routine calculations.

The preceding Logatronic had supplied the technical starting point. It had been introduced at the 1965 Hanover Fair as a desk-sized machine built on a modular plan and using semiconductor electronics. The decision to put Müller’s independent design into production had taken encouragement from Müller’s wife, because Nixdorf doubted whether the engineer could carry out the task. The resulting product became the company’s first commercially successful computer for Müller.

The system’s sales created the basis for a change in the company’s position. Kienzle in Villingen and Ruf-Buchhaltung Hegnauer & Heilmann in Karlsruhe produced versions under their own names and marketed them across Germany. Nixdorf’s direct distribution organization brought the company into contact with business customers beyond its established office-machine partners. In April 1968, Nixdorf acquired a majority of Wanderer AG for eight million Deutsche marks. The combined businesses formed Nixdorf Computer AG that October, with Wanderer’s nationwide sales organization, production capacity, and electromechanical expertise.

events.title: Forms Nixdorf Computer AG
events.description: In April 1968, Heinz Nixdorf acquires a majority of Wanderer AG for eight million Deutsche marks. The purchase gives his Laboratory for Impulse Technology access to Wanderer’s development, production, and nationwide sales organization. On October 1, the combined business becomes Nixdorf Computer AG.

events.title: Wins American Production Order
events.description: In 1969, Heinz Nixdorf travels to the United States to seek new sales opportunities after acquiring Wanderer AG. In Chicago, Victor Comptometer orders 10,000 Conti calculating machines from the Wanderer works. The order is worth 100 million Deutsche Mark. Wanderer expands its production capacity to fill it.

events.title: Reaches Twenty-Two Countries
events.description: By 1972, Nixdorf Computer AG operates in 22 countries from its base in Paderborn. Its electronic calculators and computers serve banks, supermarkets, industrial companies, and health insurers. Large American computer manufacturers largely ignore this market.

events.title: Builds Paderborn Production Campus
events.description: In 1974, Nixdorf begins building modern production facilities in Paderborn. The company also builds its headquarters in the city’s Paderauen area.

events.title: Expands Employee Sports Program
events.description: In 1979, Heinz Nixdorf brings Kurt Bendlin to Nixdorf Computer AG in Paderborn as head of training and sports support. Bendlin had held the world record in the [[decathlon]] and won an Olympic bronze medal. He organizes physical training for the company’s employees. Nixdorf makes sport part of employee development.

decathlon.explanation: The decathlon combines ten track-and-field events, including running, jumping, and throwing disciplines. Bendlin set a world record in the event before joining Nixdorf Computer AG.

events.title: Dies at CeBIT
events.description: Heinz Nixdorf suffers a fatal heart attack while attending the first [[CeBIT|CeBIT information-technology fair]] in Hannover. He dies on the fairgrounds on March 17, 1986.
